metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.method: Static source inspection of assigned readable programs (template/programs/typescript/micro and adversarial) under frozen workload definitions. No execution/runtime timing performed by this worker; conciseness scored from source-level expressiveness per unit of semantic work, following language_quality.md fairness rules (idiomatic, non-degraded code; no algorithm substitution).
observations: MB03 (integer arithmetic mix) implemented in 61 lines including required boilerplate (declare const process/require shims needed because the frozen build compiles a single .ts file without @types/node). The core workload() function is 16 lines and directly expresses the five pinned arithmetic operations with no extra scaffolding.

TypeScript's structural typing, arrow functions, template literals, and interface destructuring keep per-operation code compact; modular reduction and floor-division expressed as single-line arithmetic without explicit casts since values stay within the safe integer range (< 2^53).

Ambient declarations for process/require (~10 lines) are an artifact of the frozen no-@types/node build recipe, not a language conciseness deficiency; identical overhead appears across all TS micro-benchmarks reviewed (mb00-mb11).

Adversarial corpus (ADV-01..26) is terse and idiomatic: most single-concept adversarial cases are under 20 lines (e.g. ADV-02_C.ts at 137 bytes), consistent with concise expression of edge-case semantics (optional chaining, nullish coalescing, discriminated unions) without extra ceremony.

Verbosity sources intrinsic to language/tooling: mandatory return-type annotations and interface declarations for structured results (Mb03Result) add a handful of lines versus a dynamically-typed language, a small syntactic cost for improved conciseness-of-intent.
metric.code_efficiency_conciseness.score_rationale: 78/100: TypeScript achieves compactness close to other C-family managed languages (Java/Kotlin) via type inference, arrow functions, and destructuring, but scores below languages with stronger expression-level constructs (e.g. Rust iterators/pattern matching or Kotlin data classes) due to residual verbosity from interface declarations, ambient declarations imposed by the frozen build recipe, and no native tuple/record shorthand.

metric.readability.method: Static source inspection of the same corpus; readability scored on naming clarity, structural decomposition, comment/documentation practice, and syntactic clarity of control flow, per language_quality.md guidance to use idiomatic, production-reasonable style.
observations: Workload files (mb00-mb11) carry frozen-spec header comments citing the exact methodology section and pinned constants, plus explanatory comments for non-obvious representability/precision reasoning (e.g. mb03.ts explains why plain number is exact and why 32-bit XOR semantics hold) -- exemplary self-documenting style enabled by TS comment conventions.

Function decomposition is clean: workload() isolates pure computation from main()'s I/O/mode-handling concerns, aided by TypeScript interfaces (Mb03Result) giving named, self-describing return shapes instead of anonymous tuples/arrays -- a readability advantage over languages lacking structural return types.
Control flow is linear and idiomatic (for-loops, no clever bit tricks substituted for pinned arithmetic), matching the requirement that no algorithmic optimizations obscure the reference computation.
Naming is consistent and descriptive (sAdd, sXor, sMul, sDiv mirror the spec's operation names) across all reviewed micro-benchmarks, aiding cross-file comparison.

Minor readability friction: ambient declare blocks and require/hrtime typings needed for the no-@types/node build add boilerplate at the top of every file that a reader must skip past to reach the actual workload logic; this is a build-harness artifact, not evidence of an intrinsically less-readable language.

Adversarial-case files are short and single-purpose, each isolating one language-edge-case (e.g. discriminated union narrowing, optional chaining), a strong readability pattern for test/adversarial code.
metric.readability.score_rationale: 82/100: TypeScript's static structural typing, interface-based return shapes, and consistent commenting conventions give strong intrinsic readability, comparable to Kotlin/Java. Slightly capped below top-tier scores due to unavoidable ambient-declaration boilerplate imposed by the frozen build recipe and TypeScript's structural (not nominal) type system occasionally requiring readers to trace shape compatibility rather than named types.
